initial_observation.encounter_context: Referred to Ophthalmology for acute onset of photophobia
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: The mother reported a 7-day history of eye blinking and rubbing, irritability, and decreased oral intake. Ophthalmological examination showed significant photophobia, epiphora, and difficulty maintaining his eyelids open. Dendritiform corneal lesions were seen bilaterally, raising the suspicion of herpetic keratitis. The mother confirmed she had been having cold sores.
known_prior_history: Born at term to a primiparous mother, following an unremarkable pregnancy
Weight gain and development were normal

evidence_items.source_text: Ophthalmological examination showed significant photophobia, epiphora, and difficulty maintaining his eyelids open. Dendritiform corneal lesions were seen bilaterally, raising the suspicion of herpetic keratitis.
A conjunctival swab and a papular, crusted, raised lesion on the thumb were each tested for HSV using a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique. Both PCRs were negative.

The presence of herpes simplex virus (HSV) had never been tested for, but the lesions responded well to valacyclovir. An Infectious Diseases consultant recommended hospitalization for intravenous acyclovir treatment.

Plasma amino acid chromatography was performed because of the presence of dentritiform corneal lesions, compatible with tyrosinemia type II (TYRII, also known as oculocutaneous tyrosinemia or Richner-Hanhart syndrome). The diagnosis of TYRII was confirmed by finding a markedly elevated plasma tyrosine level (1262 µmol/L, reference range, 40–80 µmol/L).
After 2 weeks on diet, the patient’s plasma tyrosine level was 152 µmol/L, which is mildly elevated. The corneal lesions had not recurred.

Molecular analysis further confirmed the diagnosis of TYRII, revealing 2 variants in the TAT gene, 1 from each parent: c.889C>T (p.Arg297*, a known pathogenic premature stop variant) and c.227T>C (p.Leu76Pro, not previously reported, of unknown significance, although other variants at this residue can cause TYRII).
One year later, his developmental milestones were age-appropriate.
